> 
> ```python

>             "kind_arg": True
>         }
>     ],
> ```
> 
> So when it is ret_type_arg_idx: 0 which means the return type would be same as the first arg which is array whereas in case we write return: real32, it makes the return_type as real instead of an array of type real.

```fortran
program intrinsics_74
    implicit none

    real :: x(1, 3)
    x = 0
    call random_init(.true., .true.)
    call random_number(x(1, 2))
    call random_init(.true., .true.)
    call random_number(x(1, 3))
    print *, x

    if (abs(x(1, 1) - 0.0) > 1e-5) error stop
    if (abs(x(1, 2) - 0.0) < 1e-8) error stop
    ! The two values must be the same, due to `random_init()` above
    if (x(1, 2) /= x(1, 3)) error stop
end program
```
You can just update the `intrinsics_74` test with it.

    integer :: x(4) = [1, 2, 3, 4]

    print *, shift_val
    if (shift_val /= -2) error stop

end program

Good fix. Can you show the original ASR code for the generated function? Was the `shift_val` argument `intent(in)`? If so there is another bug:
> 
> * ASR verify() must disallow the assignment to an argument if it is `intent(in)`. That would have caught this as well.
> 
> If it is not `intent(in)`, then I think we should make it.
> 
> So there are possibly two additional bugs: not `intent(in)` and verify pass not catching it. Go ahead and create issues for these two bugs as well (if the bug is there).

```
subroutine _lcompilers_cshift(array, shift, result)
    integer(4), dimension(:), intent(in) :: array
    integer(4) :: i
    integer(4) :: j
    integer(4), dimension(4), intent(out) :: result
    integer(4), intent(in) :: shift
    if (shift < 0) then
        shift = shift + ubound(array, 1)
    else
        shift = shift
    end if
    i = 1
    do j = shift + 1, ubound(array, 1)
        result(i) = array(j)
        i = i + 1
    end do
    do j = lbound(array, 1), shift + 1
        result(i) = array(j)
        i = i + 1
    end do
    return
end subroutine _lcompilers_cshift
```
This is the ASR Code for the original implementation. Does "complex" work with arrays? If so, we can use that approach. If not, we should not.

I went through the documentation of Complex intrinsic. I found that this function is not an elemental function while logical is an intrinsic elemental function.

Complex intrinsic: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-3.4.6/g77/Complex-Intrinsic.html
Logical intrinsic: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-4.7.4/gfortran/LOGICAL.html

Hence we should not provide array support for `Complex` function while we need it for `Logical`. 

```
cat a.f90 
program main
    logical :: a = .true.
    logical :: b = .false.
    print *, logical([.true., .false.], 4)
end program      
                                                                                                                                                   
gfortran a.f90 && ./a.out
 T F
```

```
cat a.f90                
program main
    print *, complex([1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0])
end program         
                                                                                                                                                  
gfortran a.f90 && ./a.out
a.f90:2:21:

    2 |     print *, complex([1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0])
      |                     1
Error: 'x' argument of 'complex' intrinsic at (1) must be a scalar
```

@certik I think the initial approach was correct wherein this function was implemented as an intrinsic function in the intrinsic function registry.
